cur:monumental-triclinium-leoninum.summary: In the apse, Christ stands on a mount among the apostles, sending them out to preach; on the left of the arch Christ enthroned gives the keys to Saint Peter (or Pope Sylvester) and a banner to Constantine, and on the right Saint Peter gives the pallium to Pope Leo III and a banner to Charlemagne. The original mosaic decorated the banqueting hall of Leo III's Lateran palace around the time of Charlemagne's imperial coronation in 800; what survives today is an 18th-century reconstruction on a new site.
facts: Pope Leo III built two great triclinia at the Lateran around 800 as the heart of papal ceremonial; their decoration carried an explicitly political message.
The present apse is a reconstruction of 1743, made after the original had been destroyed, and stands outside the Scala Santa building.
cur:monumental-triclinium-leoninum.notes: The mosaic is a reconstruction rather than the original Carolingian work, though it reproduces its composition from earlier drawings and fragments.

cur:objects-wirksworth-stone.summary: Two crowded registers of small, round-headed figures tell the Gospel story: in the upper band Christ washes the feet of Peter and the Lamb of God is shown on a cross surrounded by the evangelist symbols, and in the lower band Christ, standing in a mandorla, is carried up to heaven by angels as the apostles watch. Further scenes fill the rest of the slab. Buried face down for centuries, the stone preserves a rare Anglo-Saxon narrative cycle of Christ's saving work.
facts: Wikipedia records that the large Anglo-Saxon coffin lid was discovered under the chancel floor near the sanctuary in 1820 and is now mounted on the north wall of the nave.
cur:objects-wirksworth-stone.notes: Scene identifications are made from the photograph and follow common readings; individual scenes (e.g. the Ascension versus the Descent into Hell) are debated. Date estimates vary from the 7th to the early 9th century.

princeton:19973.summary: This small bronze pendant cross, only 4.6 cm high, has flaring arms and a suspension loop, and is decorated with lines of inlaid metal. On one face the lightly incised figure of the crucified Christ can just be made out, with his arms stretched along the cross-arms. Simple crosses like this were worn by ordinary believers as signs of faith and protection.
facts: Princeton records the inlay as silver (with a query) and dates the cross broadly to the 7th–10th century, with Syria and Palestine as places of manufacture.
According to the museum, it was said to come from Ashdod and was bought in 1932 from John Khayat.

princeton:19973.notes: The incised Crucifixion is very faint on the museum's second view and invisible on the primary image; the identification rests mainly on the museum's title.
